title: Career Roadmap — Automotive Diagnostics Technician
summary: An Automotive Diagnostics Technician identifies, tests, and troubleshoots faults in vehicle systems using diagnostic scanners, electrical testing equipment, manufacturer software, and technical service information.

blocks.text: An Automotive Diagnostics Technician identifies, tests, and troubleshoots faults in vehicle systems using diagnostic scanners, electrical testing equipment, manufacturer software, and technical service information.
With the growth of electric and hybrid vehicles, this role increasingly involves electronic control units, sensors, battery management systems, electric motors, and vehicle communication networks.

For a B.Voc Electric Vehicle Technology graduate, this is a practical, skill-oriented career pathway combining automotive electronics, EV systems, diagnostics, electrical troubleshooting, and vehicle maintenance.
Potential employers

items.text: Automobile dealerships and authorized service centres

rows.text: EV Service Trainee, Automotive Diagnostics Technician
Service Manager, Workshop Manager, Technical Training Lead

blocks.text: Progression depends on practical competence, manufacturer training, certifications, and experience.
Year 1 — Automotive and Electrical Fundamentals
Learn:

items.text: Basic electric and hybrid vehicle architecture

blocks.text: Understand the difference between conventional and electric powertrains.
EV system architecture
Traction Battery Pack
Battery Management System (BMS)
Inverter / Motor Controller
Electric Motor → Wheels
Also learn about the DC-DC converter, onboard charger, thermal management, regenerative braking, and auxiliary battery.
Year 2 — Vehicle Electronics and Diagnostic Tools
Develop practical skills in:
Automotive electronics
Diagnostic equipment
Vehicle communication
A critical skill is distinguishing the actual root cause from a symptom or stored fault code.
Year 3 — EV Diagnostics and Troubleshooting
Focus on the systems most relevant to EV service.

rows.text: State of Charge (SoC), State of Health (SoH), cell imbalance indicators
Fault codes, temperature readings, battery monitoring
Charging interruptions, connector and communication faults
Regenerative braking and electronic braking-system faults

blocks.text: Learn to document symptoms, reproduce faults safely, retrieve codes, interpret service information, test components, and verify repairs.

High-voltage safety is essential. High-voltage battery and powertrain work should only be performed after appropriate training, with approved equipment and manufacturer procedures. Do not open or probe high-voltage systems without authorization and the required safety controls.
Final Year — Advanced Diagnostics and Industry Readiness
Build proficiency in:
Gain hands-on exposure to at least one EV platform, ideally through a supervised service-centre internship.
A professional technician should follow a structured process rather than replacing components based only on fault codes.
1. Customer complaint and symptom verification
2. Visual inspection and safety assessment
3. Diagnostic scan and DTC retrieval
4. Live-data and electrical testing
5. Root-cause identification
6. Approved repair or component replacement
7. Clear codes and verify repair
8. Document findings and close job

Consider practical training in:

Look for recognized vocational or manufacturer-backed programs and verify that training includes hands-on assessment. A certificate alone does not establish authorization to perform high-voltage repairs.

blocks.label: EV battery diagnostics
blocks.text: Battery monitoring, cell imbalance, battery-health assessment, and BMS fault analysis.

blocks.label: Automotive electronics
blocks.text: ECUs, sensors, wiring, actuators, and communication networks.

blocks.label: Charging-system diagnostics
blocks.text: Onboard chargers, charging connectors, charging communication, and related electrical faults.

Alternative technical route:

The most valuable future skills will combine hands-on electrical troubleshooting with diagnostic software, vehicle-network knowledge, battery systems, and data interpretation.
Recommended Final Skill Stack

blocks.label: Core
blocks.text: EV architecture, automotive electronics, electrical measurements, wiring diagrams.

blocks.label: Diagnostics
blocks.text: OBD-II, DTCs, live data, CAN bus, manufacturer software.

blocks.label: EV specialization
blocks.text: BMS, battery health, charging, thermal management, high-voltage safety.

blocks.label: Professional
blocks.text: Root-cause analysis, service documentation, repair verification, customer communication.

blocks.label: Advanced
blocks.text: Oscilloscope diagnostics, telematics, Python-based data analysis, predictive maintenance.
Target profile by graduation

The student should ideally graduate with one supervised automotive or EV service internship, hands-on diagnostic-tool experience, automotive electrical troubleshooting practice, EV battery-system fundamentals, high-voltage safety training, and at least three documented diagnostic projects.

blocks.label: Best overall positioning
blocks.text: B.Voc Electric Vehicle Technology → Automotive Diagnostics Technician is a practical vocational pathway. The strongest initial combination is automotive electronics + diagnostic scanners + electrical troubleshooting + EV battery systems + CAN fundamentals + safety procedures. For long-term growth, specialize in advanced EV diagnostics, battery systems, vehicle electronics, or testing and validation.
